client: I've been really stressed about things at home lately, and I guess that's why I finally made this appointment. My partner told me last week that they feel like I'm never really "there" anymore, even when I'm physically present, and I could see how frustrated they were. I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything, since the work pressure isn't going away anytime soon, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up even when you're not sure it will help, and I'm really glad you gave this a shot. What your partner shared sounds like it landed hard — that sense of being present in body but somewhere else in mind is something so many people experience when they're carrying a heavy load, and it makes sense that it's affecting your connection. I'm curious — when you imagine being truly "there" again, what does that look and feel like to you?

client: Honestly, when I try to picture it, I get this flash of us just sitting on the couch watching something together and me actually laughing at it instead of mentally running through my to-do list. But then I immediately feel guilty, because it's like I know exactly what's missing and I'm still not fixing it. It feels further away than it should, if that makes sense.
therapist: That image of laughing together on the couch is so vivid and tender — it tells me you deeply value that connection, and that part of you hasn't gone anywhere. The guilt you're describing is really common, but I want to gently explore it with you: when you tell yourself you "should" be able to just fix it, what do you think that belief is assuming about how stress and presence actually work? What would you say to a close friend who was in exactly your situation?

client: I guess if a friend told me this I'd probably say something like, "you're dealing with a lot, cut yourself some slack." But when it's me, that just feels like making excuses, like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily. I think part of me believes that if I really cared enough, I'd just find a way to switch off the work stuff when I get home, and the fact that I can't means something is wrong with me.
therapist: You just caught something really important — you have genuine compassion available, but there's a kind of double standard where it flows freely toward others and gets blocked when it turns toward yourself. That belief that "caring enough should equal being able to switch off" is worth examining, because it treats an exhausted mind like a light switch, and that's a really harsh standard to hold yourself to. What do you think that belief might be costing you, beyond the guilt you're already feeling?

client: I think it's probably costing me any chance of actually relaxing, because even when I do have a quiet moment, there's this background hum of "you shouldn't need this, you should just be better." And I guess it also makes me pull away from my partner even more, because if I can't fix myself I don't want them to see how much I'm struggling. I can see the logic of what you're saying, but I'm not sure how you actually change a belief like that — it's not like I consciously chose to think this way.
therapist: You're absolutely right that you didn't consciously choose this belief — these patterns usually develop quietly over time, often as a way of pushing ourselves to cope, so it makes sense it feels deeply wired in. The good news is that beliefs shift not so much through willpower or deciding to think differently, but through small repeated experiences that gently contradict them — like what might happen if you let your partner see even a little of your struggle, instead of waiting until you've "fixed" yourself first. What feels like the tiniest, safest step you could imagine toward letting them in?

client: The tiniest step I can think of would maybe be just saying out loud to my partner that I'm having a hard time right now, without trying to immediately explain or solve it. But even that makes me anxious, because I worry they'll either think I'm making excuses for being distant, or they'll want to have this big deep conversation and I won't have the energy for it. I guess I'm scared that opening the door even a crack means I have to walk all the way through it right then.
therapist: That image of the cracked door is really insightful — and I want to reflect back that you actually get to decide how far it opens and when. It might even be worth telling your partner exactly that: "I want you to know I'm struggling, and I'm not ready to unpack all of it yet, but I didn't want to keep pretending everything is fine." What do you imagine might shift between you two if your partner simply heard those words, even without a big conversation following them?

client: Honestly, when I imagine actually saying those words, there's a small part of me that thinks my partner might feel relieved, like maybe they've been worried they did something wrong and this would at least tell them it's not about them. But I also can't shake the fear that it'll come across as a non-answer, like I'm dangling something in front of them and then pulling it back. I think I'd feel really vulnerable saying it and then just... leaving it there.
therapist: That flicker of hope — imagining your partner feeling relieved — is really worth holding onto, because it suggests a part of you already senses this could bring you closer rather than push them away. Vulnerability is uncomfortable precisely because we can't control how it lands, but what you're describing isn't dangling something and pulling it back — it's actually being honest about where you are right now, which is its own complete and meaningful thing. I'm wondering, what does that fear of leaving it there unresolved tell you about what you believe you owe people when you open up?

client: I think it tells me that I feel like I owe people a resolution, like if I bring something up I have to have a neat ending to offer or it's not fair to put it on them. Which is exhausting when I think about it, because it basically means I can only share something once I've already dealt with it myself, so I end up just... not sharing at all. I'm not sure where that came from but it does explain why I feel so alone with all of this.
therapist: What you just articulated is really profound — that rule "only share once it's resolved" essentially guarantees loneliness, because it means connection is only available after you no longer need it. And the fact that you can see that so clearly right now, even calling it exhausting, suggests part of you is already ready to question whether that rule is actually serving you. I'm curious — can you think of a time when someone shared something unresolved with *you*, and how did it actually feel to be trusted with that?

client: Yeah, actually — a close friend called me a few months ago just to say they were really overwhelmed and didn't know what to do yet, and I remember feeling like they trusted me enough to be in the mess with them, not just to see the cleaned-up version. It felt like a privilege, not a burden. But I think the hard part is believing my partner would feel that way about me, rather than just feeling dragged down by my problems on top of everything else they're already dealing with.
therapist: That memory is such a gift to bring into this conversation — you just described exactly what vulnerability can create between two people, that sense of being trusted with someone's real self, and you felt it as a privilege. It's worth noticing that the same compassion you extended to your friend, and that you imagined your friend extending to you, is something your partner may genuinely want the chance to offer you too. What do you think it says about how you see yourself in this relationship, that it feels easier to believe you'd be a burden than a privilege?

client: I think it probably says that somewhere underneath all of this, I don't fully believe I'm worth the effort, at least not when I'm like this, when I'm not functioning at my best. It's uncomfortable to say that out loud because it sounds so stark, but I think that's what's actually driving a lot of it. I guess I've been operating like my partner's love is conditional on me being okay, and I'm not even sure where I got that idea from.
therapist: Saying that out loud took real courage, and I want you to know it doesn't sound stark to me — it sounds like someone who just found the quiet belief that's been running the show underneath everything else. That idea that love has to be earned by functioning well is such a painful way to live, and the fact that you can now see it as a belief rather than a fact is actually a really significant moment. I'm wondering — when you think about your relationship honestly, what evidence have you seen from your partner, even recently, that might not fit that "conditional love" story?

client: When I actually think about it, my partner did reach out last week not to criticize me but to say they missed me, which isn't really what someone does if they're about to give up on you. And a few weeks before that they made my favorite meal on a night they could tell I was really low, without me even saying anything. I want to hold onto those things as evidence, but there's a stubborn part of me that keeps saying "that was then, and if they really knew how deep this goes they'd feel differently."
therapist: Those two moments — being told "I miss you" and being seen on a hard night without having to ask — are exactly the kind of evidence that deserves to be taken seriously, and it's really meaningful that you could access them. That stubborn voice saying "but if they really knew..." is worth paying attention to, because it's essentially moving the goalposts — suggesting your partner's love is only valid until they see the full picture, which keeps you permanently one revelation away from feeling safe. I'm curious — what would it mean for you, and for this relationship, if it turned out that the "deep" version of you was actually something your partner could meet and stay?
